div.head: ECf 32 B
div.ab: De heretochiis et libertate Londoniarum et uenationibus regni Britannie. Erant et alie potestates et dignitates per prouincias et patrias uniuersas et per singulos comitatus totius regni predicti constitute, qui heretoches apud Anglos uocabantur, scilicet barones nobiles et insignes, sapientes et fideles et animosi. Latine uero dicebantur ductores exercitus, apud Gallos capitales constabularii uel marescalli exercitus. Illi uero ordinabant acies densissimas in preliis et alas constituebant, prout decuit et prout eis melius uisum fuit ad honorem corone et ad utilitatem regni.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 656 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints across the page as an insertion into ECf retr. 32 (32 A–E, pp. 655–660). The dictionary cites it as “ECf 32 A …”, so it is kept with ECf here.

note.seg: auch zu Gesetzen von Aelfred, Cnut und (o. S. 553g) Heinrich I. schiebt der Londoner Herzöge ein; vgl. mein Leges Angl. S. 17. 26 (wo er sie falsch heretemii nach Quadr. Ine 15 nennt). Dieser Traum ward in der Londoner Gildhalle so populär, dass sie im 15. Jh. einen Band Liber de heretochiis nannte; Riley Munim. Gildh. Lond. I p. xvij

the Londoner also slips Herzöge (war-leaders) into laws of Alfred, Cnut and (above, p. 553, note g) Henry I; cf. my Leges Angl. pp. 17. 26 (where he wrongly calls them heretemii, after Quadr. Ine 15). This dream became so popular in the London Guildhall that in the 15th century it named a volume Liber de heretochiis; Riley, Munim. Gildh. Lond. I p. xvii
vgl. S. 657d; dass der Angelsächs. Shire regelmässig ein Ealdorman vorstand, weiss Verf. auch sonst nicht
cf. p. 657, note d; elsewhere too the author does not know that an ealdorman regularly presided over the Anglo-Saxon shire
Constabular und Marschall sind Englische Staatsbeamte seit Normannenzeit, Londoner Stadtbeamte 1264; Liber de antiq. leg. p. 61
constable and marshal are English officers of state from Norman times, London city officers in 1264; Liber de antiq. leg. p. 61

div.ab: Concerning the heretochs, and the liberty of London, and the huntings of the kingdom of Britain. There were also other authorities and dignities established throughout all the provinces and countries and throughout every shire of the whole aforesaid kingdom, who were called heretoches (army-leaders) among the English, namely barons, noble and distinguished, wise and faithful and courageous. In Latin they were called leaders of the army; among the French, chief constables or marshals of the army. They drew up the battle-lines most densely in battles and set out the wings, as was fitting and as seemed best to them for the honour of the crown and for the benefit of the kingdom.
